entries.title: City lights up downtown Chicago with official Christmas tree at Millennium Park
entries.summary: <p>Millennium Park was packed with people craning to get a look at the 50-foot tree, as it flickered to life Friday evening along with a smattering of fireworks.</p><p>The City of Chicago's 113th annual tree lighting ceremony brought out the holiday spirit, along with a host of guests, including Grammy Award-winning artist Lalah Hathaway, Knott Us Band, Ballet Chicago performing "The Nutcracker," Joshua's Troop and even Santa Claus.</p><p>This year's Christmas tree was donated by the Clark family of Campton Hills.</p><p>Music from DJ Mike P kept the party going after the 6:25 p.m. tree lighting, playing crowd pleasers like “Party in the U.S.A.” and “Wobble.”</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson and Commissioner Kenya K. Merritt joined the events hosts, ABC7 Chicago’s Ryan Chiaverini and Val Warner, at the event. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: 'It's like our living room': Montrose Saloon in Albany Park set to close after decades-long run
entries.summary: <p>All it took was one visit to Montrose Saloon for Brian Pudil, 65, and his wife to decide to move into the apartment next door. It was love at first drink.</p><p>Since then, and for the past 16 years, Pudil has gone to the bar about three or four times each week to connect with other Montrose regulars.</p><p>“It’s like our living room,” he said. “Most of us are very caring, intelligent people that are really community-minded and like to have fun”</p><p>After more than five decades, Montrose Saloon will close its doors after New Year’s Eve, the bar’s Facebook page announced Friday.</p><p>Pudil said some loyal patrons heard the news Thursday. One day later, hundreds of bar-goers and musicians flooded Montrose’s Facebook post with comments about their fond memories of and love for the venue.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> You’re in another world and just taken away from your everyday troubles,” Pudil said. “You’re in another dimension.”</p><p>The bar’s indoor space, covered with music albums and artists’ portraits, serves as a cozy spot for music lovers, while the bar’s outdoor patio operates as a family-friendly area, open to children and dogs.</p><p>According to the Saloon’s website, the Albany Park “bar on the corner” opened its doors in 1976, but those who know the bar best say Montrose has been around for decades longer.</p><p>“It opened in 1945 at least. entries.title: White Sox trade Jordan Leasure to Phillies, tender contract offers to four arbitration-eligible players
entries.summary: <p>As the deadline Friday to tender contract offers to arbitration-eligible players neared, the White Sox already had cleared out the two players who were on the bubble.</p><p>One of those players was reliever Jordan Leasure, who will miss all of next season while recovering from elbow surgery. Leasure was designated for assignment Thursday after right-hander Dustin May’s three-year, $52.5 million deal became official.</p><p>Nevertheless, the Sox found a trade partner, dealing Leasure to the Phillies for right-hander Christian Coppola, a 12th-round draft pick in July. Coppola isn’t a significant prospect at this point, but his intriguing slider eventually should find a home in the bullpen at Low-A Kannapolis.</p><p>The other was catcher Joey Bart, who was set to command an estimated $2.9 million salary in his final year of arbitration, according to MLB Trade Rumors. He was DFA’d Tuesday. The Sox needed a spot on their 40-man roster to add both infielder William Bergolla Jr. and left-hander Jaden Woods, and Bart was such an obvious candidate to depart that general manager Chris Getz openly discussed seeking a new backup catcher last week in Las Vegas.</p><p>The Sox acquired Bart in a trade in August, but his tenure with them was limited to three games by a wayward pitch that fractured a bone in his left hand. His stay in Chicago, however, will be longer. The Cubs claimed Bart off waivers Friday and agreed to terms with him on a contract for 2027.</p><p>The Sox tendered contract offers to third baseman Miguel Vargas, outfielder Brenton Doyle and relievers Huascar Brazoban and Chris Murphy, all of whom are arbitration-eligible for the first time.</p><p>The deadline for teams to agree on salaries with arbitration-eligible players normally is in mid-January, but that is likely to be delayed by a lockout.</p>

entries.title: Bulls' Caleb Wilson meets with media after hand surgery last week
entries.summary: <p>Playing “Grand Theft Auto VI” is a bit of a struggle with the brace on the right hand, but doable.</p><p>As far as when Caleb Wilson can leave Vice City and return to his full-time job as the face of the Bulls organization? The 20-year-old didn’t give a clear timetable but did make a promise.</p><p>“I’m trying to make sure my hand feels great,” Wilson said on Friday, speaking to the media for the first time since undergoing surgery last week to repair a broken hand. “I’m not going to come back and play if I feel like I’m not at my best because I’m not going to come back and be average.</p><p>“Taking it day by day, and I know in time it will feel better.”</p><p>Which should have the Bulls feeling better.</p><p>Before Wilson swiped at the basketball in Victor Wembanyama’s clutches and sustained the injury, he was everything a No. 4 overall pick in a loaded draft class was hyped up to be. The 6-foot-9 forward was averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 rebounds, and 1.8 steals per game, and learning under fire against the likes of New York, Philadelphia and Boston – two times each.</p><p>Now he’ll have to learn from the bench with street clothes on, as the original timetable released from the team was four-to-six weeks.</p><p>“A lot,” Bulls coach Tiago Splitter replied when asked what Wilson can take away from the team as a spectator. “How you react to everything, you see the struggles and also the enjoyment of just being with his teammates and going through the ups and downs of the game. I think that’s important. There are a lot of little things that happen during a game – small conversations, timeouts – a lot he can learn from.</p><p>“He’s a rookie, he just got here. It might be different if you’re a 15-year vet. He’s got to absorb everything he can to get better.”</p><p>Surprisingly, not a real stretch for Wilson. While his personality is that of a high-energy go-getter who expects greatness from himself, he had the game taken away from him last season at North Carolina when he broke his left hand and missed the NCAA Tournament run.</p><p>A hard lesson learned then.</p><p>This latest hand injury is a bit different in his eyes. It’s not season ending or close to it, and he knows that while there is no substitute to playing, there’s still a lot he can take away that he needs improvement in.</p><p>“It’s difficult, but it’s not long term,” Wilson said. “I’ll play again in a couple weeks, so I’m not really worried about it. It gives me an opportunity to get in shape more, see the game from a different view on the bench. I’m excited. I’m going to get stronger, I know what I need to get better at because I played against such great teams so early, so it’s exciting for me.”</p><p>Splitter hopes he does continue visually learning from a far and doing so in a suddenly winning culture. The Bulls went 3-1 in their first four games without Wilson, as Matas Buzelis has really stepped up in his absence.</p><p>That of course has led to the conspiracy theory that the Bulls – and specifically Buzelis – could somehow be better with Wilson short-term, and Splitter did his best to put that to rest.</p><p>“Two things: I think we are playing as a team better in terms of just getting used to what we need to do,” Splitter said. “Also, maybe Matas is having more touches now. It’s a matter of touches and confidence. I don’t think it is Matas is just playing good because Caleb is not here. When you have more touches, have the ball in your hands then naturally you’re going to have a chance to do more and feel good.”</p>

entries.title: Kam Buckner's concrete plans for House speaker
entries.summary: <p>I hate being wrong about things I’ve written. It can be horribly embarrassing.</p><p>But I actually kind of enjoy being wrong about private opinions I’ve formed that I haven’t actually shared with more than a few people. Gaining that extra bit of insight, which helps me set aside some notions that I had before, always feels like a victory to me.</p><p>And that brings us to state Rep. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/11/11/kam-buckner-illinois-house-speaker-candidate-emanuel-chris-welch-ouster-harry-benton" >Kam Buckner</a>, D-Chicago. Buckner was named House speaker pro tempore by Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, who recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/05/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-mutiny-26-democrats-call-for-new-leader-harry-benton-scandal" >announced</a> he would not seek another term after 27 of his members said they wouldn’t vote for him and it became apparent that several more held the same opinion.</p><p>Welch told me months ago that the appointment did indeed signal that Buckner was at least one of his favorites to replace him as the chamber’s leader. To me, that was a big strike against Buckner. Welch was one of now-imprisoned House Speaker Michael Madigan’s favorites, and I thought it unwise to repeat that formula this time around. A fresh start, perhaps with the state’s<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/06/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-steps-down-female-replacement-contenders" > first female legislative leader</a>? Women make up the vast majority of the House Democratic caucus, after all.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3b0000" name="module-3b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Buckner has also been one of Welch’s go-to members to tackle big projects, like the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/05/29/state-rep-kam-buckner-bears-stadium-megaprojects-bill-arlington-heights-northwest-indiana-illinois-general-assembly" >Bears stadium</a> deal and mass transit reform and funding.</p><p>Buckner did put in a lot of work with other legislators, but his bills never made it to the governor’s desk. The Senate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/31/bears-stadium-bill-springfield-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana" >refused to vote</a> on his Bears bill, and his transit bill’s funding sources were rejected by the Senate and the governor. Gov. JB Pritzker finally intervened with a somewhat “painless” funding plan that was eagerly passed by both chambers.</p><p>But then Buckner released a 15-point plan last week about how he would govern if elected House speaker. My associate Isabel Miller wrote about it for our subscribers, and I was quite impressed with the thought and care Buckner put into his proposal.</p><p>To be clear, I’m not in any way endorsing Buckner’s candidacy. That’s up to the House. But I do strongly believe that many if not all of his ideas ought to be incorporated or at least addressed by whomever does win the top job.</p><p>“The speaker’s first job is not to accumulate power, but to share it,” Buckner told colleagues in his email. What a novel and encouraging concept that is.</p><p>More from Isabel’s story:</p><p>“On legislation, Buckner wants policy development, negotiations and oversight moved back into standing committees, reducing reliance on working groups. Subcommittees would gain explicit authority to hold hearings, examine legislation and formally recommend action to their parent committees.”</p><p>The working groups have gotten way out of hand. They do all their work in private, rarely involve the Senate and the governor’s office and members tend to wait until the last minute to unveil their final project, when it’s too late for the other chamber to weigh in.</p><p>“The plan would give deputy House majority leaders specific assignments, such as labor, infrastructure or education, with authority and responsibilities beyond their titles. Buckner also wants stronger independent House budget analysis; revenue forecasting; policy research and oversight, including a return to adopting legislative revenue estimates — lawmakers’ assessment of how much money is available to spend.</p><p>“As he has said before, Buckner would eliminate the internal 60-vote rule, which requires sponsors to demonstrate enough support to pass legislation before it reaches the floor. That would not guarantee every bill a vote. Buckner says members would remain responsible for building support, while the speaker would have to explain why a bill could not advance and identify a path forward when one exists.</p><p>“’No member should spend weeks working a roll call for legislation that leadership has already determined will not advance,’” he wrote.</p><h3>More proposals for change</h3><p>Buckner also wants to establish a procedure for removing a member from the Democratic caucus. Welch abruptly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2025/05/16/emanuel-chris-welch-fred-crespo-ouster-house-commitee-seperate-budget-rich-mller" >kicked</a> state Rep. Fred Crespo, D-Hoffman Estates, out of the caucus for using House resources to develop some alternative budget ideas — many of which Welch and the other leaders used to balance the budget.</p><p>“Technology upgrades would include a member app, bill tracking, digital documents and automated notifications. Members would receive communications plans tailored to their districts, with regional media expertise and help with local newspapers, digital content and op-eds,” Isabel wrote.</p><p>The House Democrats are far behind in all of those areas, mainly because of lack of funding and imagination.</p><p>And Buckner would change the way staff complaints against members are handled, which was one of the straws that broke the camel’s back with Welch. He wants protections for whistleblowers, clear workplace standards and independent reporting channels, some of which he details in his letter.</p><p>There’s lots more, so I encourage you to follow this link: <a class="Link" href="https://49h7k5kab.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=001QFL8IIP9y3nwbSofWDeWov-jVbHnxvCzl3tzu-hLe-f6KLB7ZFdMq-SGDL5sVSGpBULjXEZ_jhYfeuEWX93B5iT-LnYimIEse_bIjQA-Xp9rlMH0kPJrX445O9FPNyNnJa-rV3XZ04MfwksI4i6Jig==&c=vWuW_0k2vJ4Cnt5RRHTrtucPcWsjehMnPEh8kwSVhbwIFdI2VYAvoA==&ch=sRL9OIl89a3C5NZ7xnURo-SqDpr3l5Qu_Un501s-AvrNeViVYA6ryA==" target="_blank" >shorturl.at/jDGU6</a></p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-360000" name="module-360000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Third man arrested, charged in 2025 Belmont Cragin fatal stabbing
entries.summary: <p>A 21-year-old man was charged in connection with a fatal stabbing in the Belmont Cragin neighborhood last year, Chicago police said.</p><p>Emmanuel Martinez was arrested Wednesday in the 10200 block of South 76th Avenue and charged on three felony counts of murder and a single count of mob action involving force by two or more people, according to a police news release.</p><p>Martinez was identified as a suspect in the June 7, 2025 stabbing death of Yahir Viveros-Alarcon, 27, in the 5600 block of West Fullerton Avenue, police said.</p><p>Martinez is the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/11/second-man-charged-in-fatal-belmont-cragin-stabbing" target="_blank" >third suspect arrested </a>in the killing, including Jose Ramos, 25, who was charged with first-degree murder and mob action on Nov. 11, along with Sergio Vargas, 29, apprehended and charged on the same counts in November 2025.</p>

entries.title: Josh Giddey at point guard? This experiment is not going to end well
entries.summary: <p>So, here we are.</p><p>At the intersection between the small difference between experiment and theory. The Josh Giddey crossroads. Where drama surrounding his existence in a Bulls uniform is beginning to metastasize.</p><p>Experiments, if given the chance, should, by nature, be given the chance to be and end wrong. That doesn’t mean they are wrong; it just means a different or other route needs to be taken to get to the conclusion sought. To make the experiment not become an enigma.</p><p>Giddey running the point for the Bulls is an experiment. Year 3 is so far proving to be his Stage 5, the ‘‘Analyze Data and Draw Conclusion’’ part. The precursor to (the Bulls) facing a conclusion. Even as his 18-point, 14-rebound, nine-assist, four-turnover ‘‘bounce-back from the fourth quarter benching’’ game Wednesday showed the type of player Giddey needs to be for the Bulls to discover whom they can become, the inconsistency and unknowing of when another game like that will happen is equivalent of Giddey not saving himself from himself.</p><p>A CHGO Sports podcast clamped down on Giddey like Payton Pritchard in the Boston game and targeted him like most defenses seem to be doing whenever he has the rock: ‘‘The effort, the compete level was not there in a way it needed to be.’’ ‘‘It’s never good when my starting point guard in the fourth quarter of a game is unplayable.’’ ‘‘Is this guy good enough to lead your team when you’re playing at the highest level? From what I’ve seen this year . . . I don’t see it.’’ ‘‘I would like a real point guard on my team, please.’’</p><p>Between Matt Peck, Will Gottlieb and Big Dave Watson, the theory of Giddey was on full blast. ESPN apparently (according to Bulls Central) didn’t help by saying Giddey was (possibly) not in executive vice president Bryson Graham’s plan and instigating the term ‘‘bridge player’’ into his situation.</p><p>Of the fourth quarter benching, Giddey’s ‘‘ . . . that’s a point guard’s job. If I can’t do that, I probably shouldn’t be a point guard’’ comments he made about himself Monday that got points for his 100% realness somehow missed the credit that should have come with it for being the truth. As he may hold the answer to the conclusion of his own experiment.</p><p>The theory is that it’s the turnovers. It’s not just the turnovers; it’s more than that. Through the games so far that have made up this Bulls season, Giddey has fallen below his career ‘‘C-level’’ averages in other areas: field-goal and three-point percentages down, free-throw percentage way down, win shares down to below the fault line (-0.1), points and rebounds down, PER down.</p><p>All of which, when you compare his turnover average this season with his career average (3.3 versus 2.9), doesn’t come off as drastic as the conversation seems to be making it out to be.</p><p>Still, here we are.</p><p>The why of this trial (and error) run is a different piece of rhetoric. One that falls under the same ominous cloud as the Noa Essengue Experiment, the Patrick Williams Experiment, last season’s draft-deadline experiment — which included the horrific four-game, two-month Jaden Ivey Experiment and the miserably failed Ayo Dosunmu Experiment the Bulls decided to end before completion — if they fail to play this smart.</p><p>Like scientists instead of coaches and executives.</p><p>What cannot be overlooked, overstated enough or misunderstood in any way in this is the role playing alongside Coby White and Dosunmu had on Giddey’s play at the point during their tenures here. While Giddey ran the point during the last two seasons, the full responsibility of doing it was never all on him. Now it is. Which is a whole other ballgame.</p><p>Uncomfortable is what he is, theoretically. What he has been inside this experiment. The Bulls are forcing him to be something he’s not. Like the Bears did Devin Hester at wide receiver. It’s not that Giddey can’t play point, he just hasn’t found the way to do it without losing his entire style of play and the benefits that come with that. He also has not yet found anyone to lead him the right way into that transition. Which is coming at both the team’s and his expense.</p><p>Maybe he should call Ty Jerome and ask what’s the secret. A visit to the NBA psychological alchemist Iren Rainey, maybe?</p><p>An improbable half-court, game-ending, buzzer-beater in 2025 at the UC to beat the LeBron/Luka-led Lakers that will go down as his career promise. A shot by Giddey that, at the time, was believed (or desperately taken) to be the beginning of the Bulls’ return to (any) meaningful basketball-related conversation.</p><p>What was lost in his 25-point, 14-rebound, 11-assist performance that night against the Lakers were the seven turnovers he accumulated running the offense. From there, it has been — or seems to have been — a slow, inconsistent decline for Giddey since.</p><p>The jagged big pill that now must be swallowed: The Josh Giddey Experiment is an experiment gone wrong. He’s not wrong (as a player), the Bulls aren’t wrong (as a team for experimenting), he’s just the wrong player to be the orchestrator of this symphony. They both know they need to realign their whole line of thinking.</p><p>Yet, here we are.</p>

entries.title: Bulls fall in NBA Cup pool play but added a new starter to the lineup
entries.summary: <p>On a night when the Bulls were finally able to move Nic Claxton into the starting lineup, inching closer to being whole, the visiting Wizards already had a foundation piece in the middle of their lineup.</p><p>And unfortunately for the home team, Anthony Davis wasn’t on any sort of minutes restriction.</p><p>That was bad news for the Bulls, as Davis went off for 36 points and 11 rebounds, giving Washington the 98-94 win in an important Group C pool play game for the NBA Cup.</p><p>The bad taste to come out of the loss, however, wasn’t just what Davis did, but what the Bulls (4-11) didn’t do. Specifically, blowing a first-half lead by scoring just nine third-quarter points and still having a chance to take the lead with 21.8 seconds left in the game off a Claxton rebound.</p><p>The ball found its way into Norman Powell’s hands, who at first looked to have the space for a three down 96-94, but rather than try and play hero, drove the lane for his patented floater, only to watch it rim out and into the hands of Wizards veteran Khris Middleton with 6.3 seconds left.</p><p>“I liked the matchup I had, attack the paint,” Powell said of the play. “I saw Trae (Young) close on me super hard but I didn’t want to foul bait. I saw the drive and took the floater I’ve been taking since I was a kid. Just in and out.”</p><p>Which also dropped the Bulls to 1-2 in pool play, all but ending any hopes of capturing a wildcard.</p><p>As for the bigger picture, Claxton is likely headed for the starting lineup on a permanent basis, scoring 11 points and grabbing seven rebounds.</p><p>Acquired in a four-team trade back in July, Claxton suffered a hamstring injury right before fall camp started and was laid up through the first eight games of the regular season. He finally made his Bulls debut off the bench, and of course with minutes restrictions, two weeks ago against the 76ers.</p><p>With Jalen Smith a scratch Friday morning because of an illness, Claxton was the obvious choice to jump into the starting lineup.</p><p></p><p><b>Cup runneth over</b></p><p></p><p>The NBA Cup hasn’t been every coach’s cup of tea, especially the idea of point differential being a decider in the tiebreaker and that leading to some scores being run up at times.</p><p>Coach Tiago Splitter, however, was admittedly a fan of the in-season tournament.</p><p>“I like it, I really do,” Splitter said. “Right now people don’t give it the attention as far as what it means, but I think in the future it could be a bigger and bigger tournament.”</p><p></p><p><b>In the eyes</b></p><p></p><p>Caleb Wilson admitted on Friday that he was a believer in visualization, so the idea that he gets to sit on the bench while his hand heals and put himself into different actions and positions can only help his game.</p><p>“Every situation you’ve got to put yourself in the shoes of the situation that’s happening so of course I put myself in the shoes of, ‘Hey that was a nice move,’ or ‘I like what you did there,’ “ Wilson said. “I can put it in my repertoire. Most of the game is mental.”</p><p></p><p><b>Staying power</b></p><p></p><p>Noa Essengue played one of his better halves against the Wizards, scoring eight points. But the key was limiting his fouls. The second-year forward had just one going into the halftime locker room. Splitter credited a lot of film for Essengue.</p><p>“He knows, he understands,” Splitter said. “When you watch film with him he says the right things. It’s a matter of time, a matter of how many games is he going to need to know this and get better?”</p>
